intro: Every game needs a place. Towns share parks, gyms and lighted fields. Boston set aside its Common in 1634. Chicago joined 22 park districts into one in 1934. People pay taxes so everyone can use these places.

Every game needs rules too. Long ago, a stone line at Olympia showed runners where to start. Later, clubs wrote rules on paper. The Football Association formed in London in 1863. The IHSA began in Illinois in 1900.
In this unit, you will name places that towns built for play. You will tell who wrote a rule and when. You will explain how a line or a short rule helps strangers play together.
bigQuestion: Who builds the places for play, and who writes the rules that strangers share?

timeline.t: Greek tradition dates the first race at Olympia
An order bans football in the streets of London
The Knickerbocker club writes 20 baseball rules
The Football Association forms in London
Chicago names Lincoln Park for President Lincoln
Naismith starts basketball in a Springfield gym
The Illinois High School Association begins
The Chicago Park District is formed
First major league night game, in Cincinnati
Wrigley Field turns on lights for night games

words.d: land that belongs to everyone in a town
a local government that runs parks, pools and playing fields
money people pay to a government to share the cost of things everyone uses
a room or building for exercise and games; short for gymnasium
a building in a park with a gym and other rooms for the neighborhood
a line where a race begins
an old story many people tell that may not be true
written rules that members of a group agree to follow

test.q: Which city set aside a public park in 1634?
test.why: Boston set aside Boston Common in 1634.

test.q: What joined together in Chicago in 1934?
test.why: In 1934, 22 park districts joined to form the Chicago Park District.

test.q: What did Naismith use as the first goals?
test.why: Two peach baskets hung 10 feet high in the Springfield gym.

test.q: What happened at Wrigley Field in 1988?
choices: it got lights for night games
test.why: Wrigley Field added lights in 1988, last in the major leagues.

test.q: Where is an ancient stone starting line still in the ground?
test.why: The stone starting line is still at Olympia.

choices: an old story that may not be true
test.why: The Doubleday baseball story is a legend. Historians found no proof.

test.q: Where did the Football Association form in 1863?
test.why: Clubs met at the Freemasons' Tavern in London on 26 October 1863.

test.q: What shape was Wingfield's first tennis court?
test.why: It was narrow at the net and wide at the back.

test.q: Who keeps soccer's Laws of the Game?
test.why: IFAB has kept the Laws of the Game since 1886.
The Illinois High School Association began in 1900.

write.prompt: Pick one place from this unit, like Boston Common, a Chicago fieldhouse or Wrigley Field. Pick one rule book, like the 1863 football laws or the IHSA by-laws. Tell or draw who made each one and in what year.
tips: Name the place and the year it began.
Say who can use the place.
Draw a real place you know, with no team logos.
